body:
We discussed this in the team sync today and think reducing the `fetch_shard_store` threadpool (perhaps to `1`) on nodes with spinning disks would be a good thing to try, although we have seen cases where even a single thread reading metadata can be too much.

Adrien led us to the observation that checksums may be the wrong things to be looking at in the replica shard allocator too, since we really transfer segments and not files. Maybe we should identify the segments directly, perhaps using their unique IDs, which I think can be done with a good deal less IO.

We will experiment with reducing the threadpool size as a first step and come back to the other ideas later.
https://discuss.elastic.co/t/warm-nodes-on-spinning-disks-not-stable-falling-out-of-cluster-during-recovery/250078 looks to be an instance of this.

On closer inspection this behaviour is particularly bad if using `index.store.preload` since we open each file afresh. If the file is subject to preloading then opening it will also read it entirely into physical memory, even though we only care about the checksum in the last few bytes.

Therefore as well as reducing the size of the `fetch_shard_store` threadpool to `1` it will also help not to use `index.store.preload`.

issue.title: Do not mmap() or preload files just for the footer

issue.body:
Today during replica shard allocation we read the checksum footer for
every file (#56933). By default some of these files are opened using
`mmap()` and are subject to preloading if preloading is configured. This
is rather wasteful.

This commit switches these open-and-read-footer operations to use
`NIOFSDirectory` avoiding the unnecessary preloading step even if it is
configured. This somewhat mitigates #56933, but does not resolve it
fully since even after this change we still open many more files than we
really need to.

body: It turns out that as part of the searchable snapshots work we already did most of what was needed to avoid preloading in this context in 7.x. I did the last bit in #65917 so now this is just about the excessive number of files that get opened.
